title: Ride-hailing dispatch
brief: You run dispatch for a big metro area. About 100,000 drivers send a position every 4 seconds, and riders ask for cars near them. When a stadium empties, thousands of riders ask for a car from the same few blocks at the same moment. Match riders to drivers fast, and never charge a trip twice.

clarify.q: How accurate must the car positions be?
clarify.a: A rider sees cars that are a few seconds old. Dispatch itself needs the freshest position of each driver.

clarify.q: What happens at a stadium exit?
clarify.a: Thousands of requests come from one small area in a few minutes. One map cell can get a third of all lookups.

clarify.q: Can a ride request be lost?
clarify.a: No. Once a rider is told a car is coming, the trip record must survive a server failure.

clarify.q: Is a duplicate charge ever acceptable?
clarify.a: Never. A trip is charged once, even if the network retries.

requirements.users: 15 million riders and 600,000 drivers a month, 100,000 drivers online at peak (approx.)
notes: 100,000 drivers x one ping per 4 s is about 25,000 pings a second. Locations are 80 percent of traffic.
Rider reads are nearby-car lookups and price quotes. Writes are ride state changes: request, accept, start, end.
Notification speed measures provider acceptance. Device receipt is outside this traffic model; check expiry, provider outcome and retries in the correctness trace before claiming delivery guarantees.

numbers.label: Driver pings per second at peak
Ride writes per second at peak
Write shards needed at about 2,000 writes/s each, with room to spare
numbers.how: 1,200 / 2,000 = 0.6 of one shard; four shards give headroom and a failure margin

hints: Location pings are four out of five requests and each one is tiny. Do they belong in the same database as ride records?
Keep positions in a store built for many small writes, behind a socket gateway. Put a short-lived cache in front of nearby-car lookups, because one map cell can become a hot key.

Balancer, socket gateway (4 nodes) into a wide-column store for positions, 10 servers, a 5 second cache for nearby-car reads, sharded SQL for ride records, a privacy vault and key service, and an idempotency store for payments.

editorial.summary: Three workloads share one app and must not hurt each other: a firehose of tiny location writes, a read-mostly lookup that can go hot on one map cell, and a small set of rides and payments that must be exact. Split them by what each one needs.

designs.name: Firehose, hot-cell cache, careful ride records
designs.why: A socket gateway and a wide-column store take the location firehose without touching ride records. A 5 second cache serves nearby-car reads, so a stadium exit hits memory and not the database. Ride records go to sharded SQL with synchronous copies, and the payment call is guarded by an idempotency store.

tradeoffs: Reading a position back with consistency level ONE is fast and can be a few seconds stale. A driver position is stale after 4 seconds anyway.
A 5 second cache means a rider can see a car that just took another trip. The match step re-checks with the driver before it commits.
Sharding ride records by city or map region keeps each shard small, and makes a trip that crosses regions need extra care.
Running every layer in three zones costs about a third more and is what lets one zone fail at rush hour with no outage.
A privacy vault costs about $1,000 a month and is what lets you answer a data-protection audit in minutes.
editorial.realWorld: Large ride apps track millions of drivers worldwide with a position every few seconds, and divide the map into small cells (hexagons or squares) so each region can be handled on its own (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Ride-hailing dispatch: A worker sends a message, then crashes before recording success. What key and delivery states would you store so a retry does not send it twice?
correctness.discussion: Give each logical message a stable key, scoped to its recipient and channel, and enforce a unique constraint on that key. Save the request and an outbox entry in one transaction, then track pending, sending and delivered states. A queue alone does not prevent duplicates. If the provider accepts the send but the worker crashes, retry with the same provider idempotency key or query its status. Without provider support, exactly-once external delivery cannot be guaranteed: discuss whether a possible duplicate or a possible missed message is acceptable.

fields.label: The provider accepts the operation, then the worker crashes before saving success. What state is durable?
options: Unknown outcome, with the original logical operation key
Failed, so the retry gets a new key
fields.explanation: Missing local success does not prove the provider rejected the operation.

fields.label: The queue redelivers that operation. What can establish one external effect?
options: Check a local cache, then send without a provider key
Reuse the provider idempotency key or reconcile its recorded outcome
fields.explanation: A local lookup and a remote side effect are not atomic. Without endpoint support, one external effect cannot be guaranteed; report uncertainty and choose an explicit recovery policy.
